attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his Substack post, written in his voice. He is not quoting anyone else.

semantics.note: A compound observation about the present as of April 2024. 'Threatened' is slightly softer than 'under siege', and 'no federal AI law' is broader than the context, which points to protective law. The contract corrects that reading. The 'thrall' part is emphatic, close to rhetoric.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary and fair. 'Law' is read as protective federal legislation, as the surrounding paragraph implies. 'Thrall' is read as undue influence, 'under siege' as actual AI-driven attempts to disrupt elections, and 'everywhere' as widespread. The outcome comes from gaps in the evidence, not from how the words are read.

evidence.note: FCC commissioner's statement, Feb 2024. It documents the New Hampshire voice-cloning robocalls that urged voters to stay home, which supports the election component. It also mentions voice-clone scams, but gives no measure of how widespread they were.
FBI alert, June 2023, on deepfake sextortion and a rise in reports. It covers an earlier period and gives no prevalence figure for April 2024.
DHS announcement, Apr 26 2024, naming tech CEOs to an advisory board. It shows industry access, not undue influence over policy.
Senator's release, Apr 16 2024, showing AI election bills still awaiting markup. This gives limited support to the legislative component, but it is not a complete check of the statute book.
FCC ruling applying an existing 1991 statute to AI voices. Under the contract this is action under existing law, not new protective AI legislation, so it does not contradict the claim.

reviews.rationale: Only the election part is shown: the New Hampshire voice-clone robocalls (e1). Bills pending in April 2024 (e4) suggest no protective law had passed, but the packet admits it has no full inventory of statutes. Nothing measures how widespread deepfake scams were, and the DHS board (e3) shows access, not undue influence. Nothing contradicts any part, but the support condition needs all four parts, so the packet does not settle the claim.
